sections.b: Luke gives the Lord's Prayer as Jesus' answer when a disciple, having watched him pray, asks to be taught as John taught his disciples (Luke 11:1). His form is shorter than Matthew's: it opens with "Father" alone, has five requests instead of seven, asks God to "keep giving us each day our bread," and prays for forgiveness of "sins" while keeping the language of debt ("everyone who owes us"). The oldest manuscripts of Luke lack "may your will be done" and "rescue us from the evil one"; later scribes added them from Matthew. Luke follows the prayer with the friend at midnight and the promise that the Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask (Luke 11:5–13), so that the prayer comes with a lesson in bold confidence.

common: The Lord's Prayer as Christians pray it comes from Matthew's longer form, with a closing doxology found in the Didache and later manuscripts of Matthew.
uncommon: A few scholars think the request "May your Holy Spirit come upon us and cleanse us," found in two late manuscripts of Luke 11:2 and known to Gregory of Nyssa, is Luke's original wording.

sections.b: Luke shows Jesus praying at every turning point: at his baptism, before choosing the Twelve, before Peter's confession, at the transfiguration, on the Mount of Olives and on the cross (Luke 3:21; 6:12; 9:18, 28–29; 22:41–44; 23:34, 46). In Luke 11 a disciple sees him praying and asks to be taught. Jesus gives the Lord's Prayer, the parable of the friend who knocks at midnight, and the command to keep asking, looking and knocking, ending with the promise that the Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask (Luke 11:1–13). Luke returns to the theme with the widow and the unjust judge and the Pharisee and the tax collector (Luke 18:1–14). Acts continues it: the church waits for the Spirit in prayer (Acts 1:14).

sections.h: The Father gives the Spirit to those who ask
sections.b: Where Matthew says the Father gives "what is good" to those who ask (Matthew 7:11), Luke says he gives the Holy Spirit (Luke 11:13). The Spirit is one of Luke's great themes, from the births of John and Jesus to Pentecost. Luke 12 adds two sayings: speaking against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven (Luke 12:10), and the Spirit will teach disciples what to say when they are put on trial (Luke 12:11–12). Acts shows both promises at work: the Spirit comes to praying believers (Acts 1:14; 2:1–4; 4:31), and Peter and Stephen speak before the council filled with the Spirit (Acts 4:8; 6:10).
sections.refs: Luke 11:13; Luke 12:10–12; Matthew 7:11; Acts 2:1–4; Acts 4:8; Acts 4:31; Acts 6:10

sections.h: The strong man and the stronger one
sections.b: In Luke 11:14–26, when Jesus' critics say he drives out demons by Beelzebul, he answers that a kingdom split against itself falls, and that he works "by God's finger," the phrase of the exodus plagues (Exodus 8:19). Satan is pictured as a strong man guarding his courtyard in full armor; Jesus is the stronger one who overpowers him and divides the spoils, an image from Isaiah 49:24–25. In Luke 13:16 a woman bent double for eighteen years is called one "whom Satan has kept tied up," and her healing on the Sabbath is a release from his bond. Luke's Jesus has seen Satan fall (Luke 10:18), and Acts sums up his ministry as healing "all those the devil was crushing under his power" (Acts 10:38).
sections.refs: Luke 11:14–26; Luke 13:16; Luke 10:18; Exodus 8:19; Isaiah 49:24–25; Acts 10:38

sections.b: Luke 11:20 is one of the strongest sayings for the kingdom's presence: "if it is by God's finger that I throw out demons, then God's kingdom has already reached you." Yet the same chapter teaches disciples to pray "May your kingdom come" (Luke 11:2), and Luke 12:32 promises that the Father has delighted to give them the kingdom. In Luke 13 the kingdom is a mustard seed that grows into a tree for the birds and yeast hidden in three measures of flour (Luke 13:18–21), and its final form is a feast where people come from every direction and sit with Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and the prophets (Luke 13:28–29). Scholars from C. H. Dodd onward have debated how "already" and "not yet" fit together; Luke keeps both.

Luke gives the most mixed picture of the Pharisees among the Gospels. In Luke 11:37–54 a Pharisee invites Jesus to a meal, is surprised that he does not wash first, and hears three woes on Pharisees and three on lawyers: for cleaning the outside of cups while neglecting the inside, for tithing herbs while passing over justice and the love of God, for loving honor, and for burdening others. The issues are real Pharisaic practices, and Jesus does not dismiss them ("These you should have done," Luke 11:42). The meal ends with scribes and Pharisees hunting for a word to use against him (Luke 11:53–54), and Jesus warns his disciples against their yeast, hypocrisy (Luke 12:1). Yet in Luke 13:31 some Pharisees warn Jesus that Herod wants to kill him, and in Acts Pharisees defend the apostles and join the church (Acts 5:34–39; 15:5).

common: Luke's woes in 11:37–54 have often been read as a rejection of Judaism as legalism, a reading that scholars of ancient Judaism such as E. P. Sanders and Amy-Jill Levine have shown to be unfair to the Pharisees.

sections.h: Luke's "between the altar and the house"
sections.b: Luke's form of the saying (Luke 11:50–51) has no father's name, so it raises none of the questions of Matthew's "son of Berechiah" (Matthew 23:35). Luke places the murder "between the altar and the house," that is, in the temple court before the sanctuary, as 2 Chronicles 24:21 says. The verb "called to account" (ekzēteō, "seek out") echoes Zechariah's dying words, "May the LORD see it, and may he seek it out" (2 Chronicles 24:22). Later Jewish legend told that his blood kept seething in the temple until the Babylonian conquest (Babylonian Talmud Gittin 57b), a sign of how deeply his murder was remembered.

sections.h: The rich fool and treasure in heaven
sections.b: Luke 12 is one of the Bible's fullest teachings on possessions. A man asks Jesus to make his brother share an inheritance; Jesus refuses and warns against every kind of greed, because life does not come from what one owns (Luke 12:13–15). The parable of the rich fool follows: a man who builds bigger barns for a bumper crop, plans years of ease, and hears God say, "On this very night they demand your soul back from you" (Luke 12:20). Jesus then tells the disciples not to worry about food or clothing, to seek the kingdom, and to "Sell your property and give alms" for a treasure in heaven (Luke 12:22–34). The theme recalls Ecclesiastes and Sirach on wealth left to others (Ecclesiastes 2:18–21; Sirach 11:18–19).

claude.title: Claude's theory: three barns
claude.body: Commentators already link the rich fool's barns (Luke 12:18) with the ravens that have none (Luke 12:24). My suggestion, set out on the Luke 12 page, goes one step further: the "pouches that never get old" (Luke 12:33) are a third barn, the only storehouse that lasts.

sections.b: Jesus' teaching in Luke 12 grounds trust in God's detailed care. Five sparrows sell for two small coins, yet God does not forget one, and the hairs of the disciples' heads are counted (Luke 12:6–7). God feeds the ravens, unclean birds that have no storeroom or barn, and dresses the wildflowers that will be oven fuel tomorrow (Luke 12:24–28), as the Psalms and Job say (Psalm 147:9; Job 38:41). From this follows the command not to worry, and the promise that the Father knows what his people need (Luke 12:29–31).
sections.refs: Luke 12:6–7; Luke 12:22–31; Psalm 147:9; Job 38:41; Matthew 6:25–34; Matthew 10:29–31

sections.b: Luke 12:35–48 pictures the time before the Son of Man's coming as a household waiting at night: slaves with robes tucked up and lamps lit for their master's return from a wedding, a householder who did not know when the thief would dig through his wall, and a manager who must feed the household while the master is away. Luke's version has the startling promise that the master will tie up his own robe and serve the watchful slaves (Luke 12:37), and Peter's question, which turns the last parable toward those in charge of others (Luke 12:41–48). Hans Conzelmann read "My master's coming is delayed" (Luke 12:45) as Luke's answer to a delayed return; others stress that Luke still calls for readiness at every watch of the night (Luke 12:38).

sections.h: The master who serves and the feast from every direction
sections.b: Two pictures in Luke 12–13 draw on the hope of the great feast of the age to come (Isaiah 25:6). In Luke 12:37 the master returning at night will seat his watchful slaves and wait on them himself, a reversal of ordinary life that Jesus acts out when he says at the Last Supper that he is like the one who waits on tables (Luke 22:27). In Luke 13:28–29 people come from the sunrise and the sunset, from the north and the south, and lie down to eat in the kingdom of God with Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and all the prophets, while those who assumed a place are outside. Luke continues the theme in the parable of the great banquet (Luke 14:15–24).
sections.refs: Luke 12:37; Luke 13:28–29; Luke 14:15–24; Luke 22:27; Isaiah 25:6; Matthew 8:11

sections.b: When people tell Jesus about Galileans killed by Pilate at their sacrifices, he refuses to call them worse sinners, and adds the eighteen killed when the tower at Siloam fell. Both times he says, "If you do not repent, you will all perish" (Luke 13:3, 5). The parable that follows, a fig tree that has borne no fruit for three years and is given one more year of digging and manure, shows God's patience and its limit (Luke 13:6–9). Earlier, Jesus holds up the people of Nineveh, who repented when Jonah preached, as witnesses against his generation (Luke 11:32), a story Jewish tradition used on fast days as the model of repentance (Mishnah Taanit 2:1).

Luke 13:1–5 is the New Testament's clearest answer to the idea that disaster proves the victim's sin. Galileans killed by Pilate and eighteen people crushed by a tower at Siloam were not worse sinners or "bigger debtors" than anyone else, Jesus says. But he turns the question into a warning for everyone: unless you repent, you will perish the same way. The same refusal appears when the disciples ask whose sin made a man blind (John 9:2–3), and it continues the protest of the book of Job against the easy reasoning of Job's friends (Job 4:7–8; 42:7).

Luke 13:1 is the only record of Pilate killing Galilean pilgrims so that their blood mixed with their sacrifices, probably at Passover, when lay Israelites slaughtered their own lambs in the temple court. No other source mentions it, but it fits the portrait of Pilate in Josephus (the standards, the aqueduct riot, the Samaritans at Gerizim) and in Philo's quoted letter, which charges him with executions without trial. Luke uses the news to call for repentance, not to condemn Pilate, who will appear again at Jesus' trial (Luke 23:1–25).

Luke's last synagogue scene is a Sabbath healing (Luke 13:10–17). Jesus frees a woman bent double for eighteen years; the synagogue leader tells the crowd that six days are for work and healing can wait. Jewish law agreed that saving life overrides the Sabbath (Mishnah Yoma 8:6), but a long-term illness was not urgent. Jesus answers from accepted practice: every one of them unties his ox or donkey to lead it to water on the Sabbath. If an animal may be untied, how much more must a daughter of Abraham be untied from Satan's bond on the Sabbath, the day that remembers Israel's release from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:15).

Luke 11–13 includes several parables found only in Luke: the friend at midnight (Luke 11:5–8), the rich fool (Luke 12:16–21) and the fig tree given another year (Luke 13:6–9). Luke's characters often speak to themselves, so the hearer overhears their hearts (Luke 12:17–19, 45). Shared with Matthew are the waiting slaves and the faithful manager (Luke 12:35–48; Matthew 24:42–51) and the twin parables of the mustard seed and the yeast (Luke 13:18–21; Matthew 13:31–33), which Luke ties to the healing of the bent woman. Each parable has a different setting in Luke than in Matthew, which shows how the same story could serve different purposes.

In Luke 13:31–33 some Pharisees warn Jesus that Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee and Perea, wants to kill him. Antipas had already imprisoned and beheaded John the Baptist (Luke 3:19–20; 9:9). Jesus calls him "this fox," a sly and petty ruler, and says he will finish his work and go on to Jerusalem. Luke alone records that Antipas later questioned Jesus during his trial (Luke 23:6–12).

sections.h: The city that kills the prophets
sections.b: On the journey, Jesus says it would not do for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem, and laments: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, killer of the prophets, stoner of those sent to her!" He longed to gather the city's children like a bird gathering her brood, but they would not, and their house is abandoned to them until they say, "Blessed is the one who comes in the Lord's name!" (Luke 13:33–35; Psalm 118:26). Luke places the lament before Jesus enters the city, so that it looks ahead to his weeping over Jerusalem and its fall (Luke 19:41–44; 21:20–24). The tower that fell at Siloam (Luke 13:4) stood in the city's southeast, near the Pool of Siloam.

Only Luke tells how a woman in the crowd cried out, "Blessed is the womb that carried you, and the breasts you drank from!" Jesus answered, "Rather, blessed are the people who hear the word of God and keep it" (Luke 11:27–28). The woman's words recall Elizabeth's blessing and Mary's own song (Luke 1:42, 48). Whether Jesus' reply corrects the woman or includes Mary as the model of those who hear and keep God's word (Luke 1:38; 2:19, 51) is read differently by the churches; see the card at Luke 11.
sections.refs: Luke 11:27–28; Luke 1:38; Luke 1:42; Luke 1:48; Luke 2:19; Luke 2:51; Luke 8:21

sections.b: Luke's Jesus twice makes alms the answer to a false security. To the Pharisee worried about clean cups, he says, "give what is inside as alms. Then, look, everything is clean for you" (Luke 11:41). To disciples tempted to store up like the rich fool, he says, "Sell your property and give alms" and make a treasure in the heavens (Luke 12:33). Luke's later stories follow the thread: Zacchaeus gives half his goods to the poor (Luke 19:8), and in Acts Tabitha and Cornelius are known for their alms (Acts 9:36; 10:2, 4).
sections.refs: Luke 11:41; Luke 12:33–34; Luke 19:8; Acts 9:36; Acts 10:2; Acts 10:4

sections.b: Luke 11–13 lies in the heart of Luke's travel section (Luke 9:51–19:44), which Luke punctuates with reminders that Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem (Luke 13:22, 33). Much of it is material Luke shares with Matthew but arranges differently: the Lord's Prayer as an answer to a disciple's request, the woes at a Pharisee's dinner table, the teaching on worry after the rich fool, the lament over Jerusalem before the entry rather than after. Luke's own contributions include the friend at midnight, the rich fool, the Galileans and Siloam, the fig tree given one more year, the bent woman and Herod "that fox." Characteristic Lukan themes run through: prayer and the Holy Spirit (Luke 11:1–13), possessions and alms (Luke 12:13–34), meals (Luke 11:37), reversal (Luke 13:30), and women as daughters of Abraham (Luke 13:16).
